notes: The San Francisco New Deal Historic Context Statement, adopted March 2023. A citywide thematic statement with no appendix inventory: its address-level material is in thirteen project tables (WPA street, bridge, parks, recreation, building and infrastructure projects; PWA school, federal and city buildings; PWAP, FAP and Treasury Section art projects), in the per-building narratives that accompany them, and in the registration and landmark-recommendation lists at the back. Most of what it names is civic — schools, playgrounds, libraries, firehouses, parks and public art — so a large share of the addresses are parcels the assessor does not carry on the secured roll.

It is City Landmark No. 286 and now houses Hilltop High School.

findings.description: The first purpose-built federal office building in San Francisco. Arthur Brown Jr., architect of City Hall, designed the four-storey granite-clad building around a central courtyard in the American Renaissance style to sit with the rest of the Civic Center. Ground was broken on 17 January 1933 before the money existed; the Public Works Administration granted $2,689,089 that August, construction began in early 1934 employing 300 men, and the building was dedicated on 16 May 1936. Staff of 33 federal agencies moved in. It was vacated in 2007 and rehabilitated in 2013.

findings.description: A sixteen-storey reinforced-concrete federal office building put up by the Public Works Administration on the site of the 1874 Appraisers Building, which was demolished in 1940. The Office of the Supervising Architect under Gilbert Stanley Underwood designed it in the PWA Moderne style; wartime rationing delayed its official opening until 1944, a year after the PWA was wound up. Its only notable ornament is an American eagle over the main entrance by Lombard & Ludwig. It was remodelled in 1985-88 by Kaplan McLaughlin Diaz and is listed in the National Register.

findings.description: The Treasury Department picked this undeveloped serpentine bluff above Upper Market Street on 2 August 1934 because vaults could be sunk into the rock. The Office of the Supervising Architect under Gilbert Stanley Underwood designed the four-storey granite-faced building in the PWA Moderne style, massed to look forbidding, its only ornament a row of parapet medallions showing the coins to be struck inside. Clinton Construction Co. built it for about $1 million from August 1935 to March 1937; it was dedicated on 15 May 1937 and began minting coins on 1 July.

findings.description: Woods Hall Annex was one of the first Works Progress Administration projects undertaken in San Francisco for the state — a science building for San Francisco State Teachers' College built from drawings W.B. Daniels had prepared in the Office of the State Architect before the state refused to fund it in 1932. Completed in the summer of 1936 with four laboratories, a dark room, offices, storage and a boiler room, in the Spanish Colonial Revival style of the rest of the campus. It holds Reuben Kadish's Federal Art Project mural A Dissertation on Alchemy, is listed in the National Register and is City Landmark No. 258; it is now the Haight Street Art Center.

findings.description: Westside Courts opened in the spring of 1943 with 136 units — four L-shaped and two U-shaped three-storey buildings arranged symmetrically around courtyards holding open space, drying yards and small play areas, with moulded concrete exterior stairs. Lester Hurd and James J. Mitchell designed it, and a 1946 survey of the city's public housing called it the most unusual and interesting design of any San Francisco Housing Authority project. It was the first public housing in the city made available to African Americans. Beniamino Bufano's granite St. Francis on Horseback, carved in 1935, was installed here in 1945.
